summary: Defines extensions to XMPP core that provide basic instant messaging and presence, meeting requirements set out in RFC 2779. It is a proposed standard and obsoletes RFC 3921.

plainLanguage.summary: This document adds the familiar chat features to XMPP: a contact list stored by the server, a rule for who is allowed to see whether you are online, and the stanzas that carry status updates and messages.

questions: what is xmpp instant messaging and presence
how do xmpp presence subscriptions work
subtitle: The XMPP extensions that provide a contact list, presence subscriptions, online status and one-to-one chat.

tldr.problem: The XMPP core defines how clients and servers exchange XML stanzas, but it says nothing about the things people expect from a chat application: a list of contacts, knowing who is online, and permission to see that information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6121 defines the roster, the presence subscription states that govern who may see whose status, the presence stanza and its show, status and priority elements, and the message stanza with its chat types. Everything is carried as XMPP stanzas over the existing core.
tldr.outcome: A client can log in, fetch its contact list, announce its availability and see that of its subscribers, and exchange chat messages. The RFC obsoletes RFC 3921 and is a Proposed Standard from March 2011.

today: RFC 6121 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2011. It obsoletes RFC 3921, and it has not been obsoleted or updated since.

sections.title: What XMPP IM Adds
sections.content:
The Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) is an application profile of the Extensible Markup Language that enables the near-real-time exchange of structured yet extensible data between any two or more network entities. The core features of XMPP provide the building blocks for many types of near-real-time applications, which can be layered on top of the core by sending application-specific data qualified by particular XML namespaces. This document defines XMPP extensions that provide the basic functionality expected of an instant messaging and presence application.

Traditionally, IM applications have combined four factors. The central point of focus is a list of one's contacts or "buddies", which in XMPP is called a roster. The purpose is to exchange relatively brief text messages with particular contacts in close to real time, often in large numbers and in rapid succession, in the form of a one-to-one chat session. The catalyst for exchanging messages is presence, that is, information about the network availability of particular contacts, so that a user knows who is online and available. And presence information is provided only to contacts that one has authorized by means of an explicit agreement called a presence subscription.

The basic syntax and semantics of XMPP were developed originally within the Jabber open-source community, mainly in 1999, and the XMPP Working Group was chartered in late 2002. Since 2004 the Internet community has gained extensive implementation and deployment experience with XMPP, including formal interoperability testing carried out under the auspices of the XMPP Standards Foundation. This document incorporates comprehensive feedback from software developers and service providers, including a number of backward-compatible modifications.
sections.plainLanguage: XMPP core gives you a way to send XML messages. This document adds what a chat program actually needs on top: a contact list, a way to publish and read online status, and permission to do so.

sections.title: How a Session Runs
sections.content:
The XMPP core specifies how a client connects to a server, and in particular the preconditions that must be fulfilled before a client may send XML stanzas, the basic unit of meaning in XMPP. These preconditions include negotiation of the XML stream, with exchange of stream headers, optional channel encryption via TLS, mandatory authentication via SASL, and binding of a resource to the stream for client addressing.

Once those preconditions are fulfilled the client has a long-lived XML stream with its server, which lets the user send and receive a potentially unlimited number of XML stanzas over the stream. Such a stream can be used to exchange messages, share presence information, and engage in structured request-response interactions in close to real time.

The typical flow for an IM and presence session is: retrieve one's roster; send initial presence to the server for broadcast to all subscribed contacts, thus going online from the perspective of XMPP communication; exchange messages, manage presence subscriptions, perform roster updates, and in general process and generate other XML stanzas with particular semantics throughout the life of the session; and finally terminate the session when desired by sending unavailable presence and closing the underlying XML stream.

RFC 3921 had specified one additional precondition, the formal establishment of an IM and presence session. Implementation and deployment experience has shown that this additional step is unnecessary, although an implementation MAY still offer the feature for backward compatibility, which lets older software connect while newer software saves a round trip.
sections.plainLanguage: Log in, fetch the contact list, send your status, then use the connection for messages and presence until you log out. The old extra handshake step is no longer needed.

sections.title: The Roster
sections.content:
In XMPP, a user's roster contains any number of specific contacts. It is stored by the user's server on the user's behalf, so the user can reach the roster information from any device. When the user adds items or modifies existing ones, if an error does not occur the server SHOULD store that data unmodified if at all possible and MUST return the data it has stored when an authorized client requests the roster. Because the roster can contain confidential data, the server MUST restrict access to it so that only authorized entities, typically limited to the account owner, are able to retrieve, modify or delete it.

Rosters are managed using iq stanzas, by means of a query child element qualified by the jabber:iq:roster namespace. Each item element describes a unique roster item. The jid attribute specifies the Jabber Identifier that uniquely identifies the roster item and is REQUIRED whenever a client or server adds, updates, deletes or returns a roster item. The name attribute is the handle associated with the JID, as determined by the user. A group element may be used to group items, and the subscription attribute records the presence subscription state.

Two attributes are set by the server rather than the client. The approved attribute with a value of "true" signals subscription pre-approval, and a server SHOULD include it to inform the client of pre-approvals; a client MUST NOT include it in the roster sets it sends, but instead MUST use presence stanzas of type "subscribed" and "unsubscribed" to manage pre-approvals. The ask attribute with a value of "subscribe" signals various subscription sub-states that include a "Pending Out" aspect, and a client MUST NOT include it, using presence stanzas of type "subscribe" and "unsubscribe" instead.

RFC 3921 assumed the only place where a user stores their roster is the server where the account is registered. This specification removes that coupling, so a user could store their roster elsewhere or have several rosters in several places, though it keeps the older terminology for now.
sections.plainLanguage: The roster is the contact list. The server keeps it so you can reach it from any device, and it decides who may read it. Some fields are the server's to set, and the client signals the same facts with presence stanzas instead.

sections.title: Roster Versioning
sections.content:
The ver attribute is a string that identifies a particular version of the roster information. The value MUST be generated only by the server and MUST be treated by the client as opaque. The server can use any appropriate method for generating the version ID, such as a hash of the roster data or a strictly increasing sequence number, and inclusion of the ver attribute is RECOMMENDED.

If a server supports roster versioning, it MUST advertise the stream feature <ver xmlns='urn:xmpp:features:rosterver'/> during stream negotiation, and that feature is merely informative and never mandatory to negotiate. If a client supports roster versioning and the server advertises support, the client SHOULD include the ver element in its request for the roster, setting the value to the version ID associated with its last cache of the roster. If the client has not yet cached the roster, or the cache is lost or corrupted, but it wishes to bootstrap the use of roster versioning, it MUST set the ver attribute to the empty string.

Whether or not the roster has been modified since the version ID the client gave, the server MUST either return the complete roster, including a ver attribute that signals the latest version, or return an empty IQ-result to say that any roster modifications will be sent via roster pushes. In general the server SHOULD send an empty IQ-result and then send the modifications via roster pushes, unless returning the complete roster would use less bandwidth than sending individual pushes, for example if the roster contains only a few items.
sections.plainLanguage: The server stamps the contact list with a version number. The client sends the version it already has, and the server answers with just the changes if nothing has moved on.

sections.title: Presence Subscriptions
sections.content:
A subscription request is a request from a user for authorization to permanently subscribe to a contact's presence information; syntactically it is a presence stanza whose type attribute has a value of "subscribe". A user's client generates a subscription request by sending a presence stanza of type "subscribe" and specifying a to address of the potential contact's bare JID. The value of the to attribute MUST be a bare JID rather than a full JID, since the desired result is for the user to receive presence from all of the contact's resources. For tracking purposes, a client SHOULD include an id attribute in the request.

The request is generated by the user's client, processed by the potential contact's server, and acted on by the contact through the contact's client. The contact can accept, refuse, or ask to see the requester's presence in return.

There are four primary subscription states, described from the perspective of the user rather than the contact. "None" means the user does not have a subscription to the contact's presence and the contact does not have a subscription to the user's. "To" means the user has a subscription to the contact's presence but the contact does not have one to the user's. "From" means the reverse. "Both" means each has a subscription to the other's presence. These are supplemented by sub-states for pending inbound and outbound requests, yielding nine possible subscription states in total, including combinations such as "None + Pending Out", "To + Pending In", "From + Pending Out" and "None + Pending Out+In".

A subscription can also be cancelled with presence stanzas of type "unsubscribe" and "unsubscribed", and a user can pre-approve an incoming request so that the subscription is granted without an explicit decision.
sections.plainLanguage: Seeing someone's status is a permission, not a free-for-all. You ask, they agree, and the two of you end up in one of four states, plus a few "waiting for an answer" variants.

sections.title: Exchanging Presence
sections.content:
Presence refers to an entity's availability for communication over a network. At the most basic level it is a boolean on/off variable that signals whether an entity is available or unavailable, the terms online and offline also being used. In XMPP, an entity's availability is signalled when its client generates a presence stanza with no type attribute, and its lack of availability when its client generates a presence stanza whose type attribute has a value of "unavailable".

XMPP presence typically follows a publish-subscribe or observer pattern, wherein an entity sends presence to its server and the server broadcasts it to all of the entity's contacts who have a subscription to the entity's presence. This kind of presence is called broadcast presence. A client can also send directed presence, a presence stanza with a to address, which is less common but is sometimes used to send presence to entities that are not subscribed to the user's presence.

After completing the core preconditions and requesting the roster, a client signals its availability by sending initial presence to its server, that is, a presence stanza with no to address and no type attribute. The user's server MUST then send the initial presence stanza from the full JID of the user to all contacts subscribed to the user's presence, and MUST also broadcast initial presence from the newly available resource to all of the user's available resources, since an entity is implicitly subscribed to its own presence. In the absence of presence information about the user's contacts, the user's server MUST also send presence probes to those contacts on behalf of the user.

The type attribute of a presence stanza selects what the stanza means. The values are error, probe, subscribe, subscribed, unavailable, unsubscribe and unsubscribed. If the value is not one of these, the recipient or an intermediate router SHOULD return a stanza error of bad-request. Clients SHOULD NOT send presence stanzas of type probe, which are generated by servers to find out the state of an entity on a peer server.
sections.plainLanguage: Your client sends your status to your server, and the server passes it to everyone allowed to see it. The same stanza type carries the subscription requests, so one small message does several jobs.

sections.title: Presence and Message Syntax
sections.content:
A presence stanza is qualified by the jabber:client or jabber:server namespace, which defines certain child elements, in particular show, status and priority. These child elements give more detail about an entity's availability and are typically included only if the presence stanza has no type attribute.

The show element specifies the particular availability sub-state of an entity or a specific resource, and a presence stanza MUST NOT contain more than one. Its character data MUST be one of four values: "away", meaning the entity is temporarily away; "chat", meaning it is actively interested in chatting; "dnd", meaning it is busy, where dnd stands for Do Not Disturb; and "xa", meaning it is away for an extended period, where xa stands for eXtended Away. If no show element is provided, the entity is assumed to be online and available. The status element contains human-readable character data, a natural-language description of availability such as "In a meeting". The priority element allows the entity to specify a numeric priority for that resource relative to the user's other connected resources.

An instant messaging client specifies an intended recipient for a message by providing the JID of the intended recipient in the to attribute of the message stanza. The type attribute of a message differentiates the common uses: "chat" for a message sent in the context of a one-to-one chat session; "groupchat" for a multi-user chat environment, similar to IRC; "headline" for an alert, notification or other transient information to which no reply is expected, such as a news headline; "normal" for a single message outside any session; "error" for a message generated after an error occurred; and "no reply", which indicates that no reply is expected.
sections.plainLanguage: Presence carries a short state, one of four values such as away or busy, plus a free-text status and a priority for that device. Messages carry a type so the program knows whether it is a chat line, a group message or a news alert.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Core security considerations for XMPP are provided in the core specification, including discussion of channel encryption, authentication, information leaks, denial-of-service attacks and interdomain federation. An XMPP user registers or has provisioned an account on a server and therefore places some level of trust in that server, so it is the server's responsibility to preferably mandate channel encryption for communication with local clients and remote servers, to authenticate any client that wishes to access the user's account, and to process stanzas on the user's behalf: storing the roster, handling subscription requests and responses, generating and handling presence probes, broadcasting presence notifications, routing outbound messages and delivering inbound ones.

Even if the server fulfils those responsibilities, the client has no assurance that the stanzas it exchanges with other clients are protected for all hops along the path, or inside the server itself. It is the responsibility of the client to use an appropriate technology for encryption and signing of XML stanzas if it wants end-to-end confidentiality and integrity.

Several rules apply only to IM and presence. When a server processes an inbound presence stanza of type probe whose intended recipient is a user of one of the server's configured domains, the server MUST NOT reveal that user's presence if the sender is not authorized to receive it as determined by presence subscriptions. A user's server MUST NOT leak the user's network availability to entities that are not authorized to know the user's presence; in XMPP itself, authorization takes the form of an explicit subscription from a contact to the user. When a server processes an outbound presence stanza with no type or of type unavailable, it MUST follow the rules of Section 4 so that presence information is not sent to entities that are not authorized to know it. A client MAY ignore the status element when it is contained in a presence stanza of type subscribe, unsubscribe, subscribed or unsubscribed, which can help prevent presence subscription spam.
sections.plainLanguage: The server is trusted with your contact list and your status, so it must not hand either to strangers. A probe asking whether you are online is refused unless the sender is allowed to know.

messages.label: PRESENCE
messages.note: Initial presence with no to address and no type, meaning available.

messages.label: PRESENCE
messages.note: Broadcast from the user's full JID to every subscribed contact.

messages.label: PRESENCE SUBSCRIBE
messages.note: Sent to the contact's bare JID.

messages.label: PRESENCE SUBSCRIBE
messages.note: The contact decides whether to accept.

messages.label: PRESENCE SUBSCRIBED
messages.note: Approval, which may also carry the contact's own presence.

items.label: available
items.desc: The entity is available for communication.

items.label: unavailable
items.desc: The entity is no longer available for communication.

items.label: request
items.desc: The sender wishes to subscribe to the recipient's presence.

items.label: approval
items.desc: The sender has allowed the recipient to receive their presence.

items.label: cancel
items.desc: The sender is unsubscribing from the receiver's presence.

items.label: refusal
items.desc: The request was denied or a granted subscription was cancelled.

items.label: probe
items.desc: A request for an entity's current presence; generated by servers.

items.label: error
items.desc: An error occurred while processing a previous presence stanza.

items.title: jid
items.text: The Jabber Identifier that identifies the roster item. Required.

items.title: name
items.text: The handle the user chose for this contact.

items.title: group
items.text: A grouping name for the item.

items.title: subscription
items.text: The presence subscription state: none, to, from or both.

items.title: ask
items.text: Set by the server to 'subscribe' while a request is pending.

items.title: approved
items.text: Set by the server to 'true' for a pre-approved subscription.

items.title: ver
items.text: The server's version identifier for the roster as a whole.
